Future of PMM Training

A Guided Learning Program for Our Product Marketing Team

Welcome

As Dan mentioned in recent Office Hours, we are embarking on a journey to transform the way we approach our jobs with artificial intelligence—both in terms of the company "becoming AI-first" and orienting around delivering agentic applications, and the way we approach our product marketing role in light of the rapidly changing business dynamics.

Our goal is nothing short of becoming the most advanced and capable AI PMM team within SAP, and paving the way for the rest of the company to adopt some of our best practices, frameworks, and tool adoption. In that spirit, we have developed a hands-on curriculum with assessments, exercises, and practical frameworks you can apply immediately. It's not a textbook to read — it's a learning journey we can complete together.

Our Point of View: The "10x PMM" isn't someone who uses AI tools to do the same job faster. It's someone who builds a co-working relationship with AI that fundamentally changes what's possible — adapting to a new funnel, a new buyer, and a new way of working.

The Three Areas of AI Development

Halfway through a Sapphire planning meeting in March, two PMMs on the same team had radically different problems.

The first — call her Maya — had been using Claude for about eight months. She'd built her own messaging-test prompt, was running a battlecard repo weekly against Klue's competitive intel feeds, was generating launch briefs in twenty minutes that used to take her three days. By every metric you'd hand a head of marketing, she was crushing it. But she'd also just drafted three competitive positioning paragraphs that got flagged as borderline non-public information — pricing logic and roadmap timing she'd pasted into a free ChatGPT account to "tighten the wording." She didn't realize the consumer-tier Terms of Service trained on her input. The team's Security partner asked her to file a self-disclosure.

The second — call him Trevor — knew SAP's AI policy cold. He'd taken every Trust Center course, could recite the data classification matrix, knew which internal LLM environment was approved for what kind of input. But Trevor was still writing his decks the way he wrote them in 2022 — outline in Word, copy into PowerPoint, format manually, three days of work. He was governance-pristine and productivity-flat. When he did try Claude, he used it for spelling and tone — the same thing he'd been using Grammarly for since 2019.

Neither Maya nor Trevor was a 10x PMM. They each had two-thirds of the equation and were missing the third in a way that completely changed the outcome.

This curriculum is built around the argument that becoming an AI-native product marketer is a three-dimensional problem. You can be technically fluent and cognitively closed off and you'll generate slop at scale. You can be cognitively integrated and tool-illiterate and your insights will never travel. You can have both and no governance instinct and you'll create the kind of incident that ends pilots and freezes adoption org-wide.

The leverage compounds only when all three move together — which is why what follows treats them as parallel tracks rather than sequential modules.

Why most AI-readiness frameworks fail: Tool vendors define readiness as tool fluency. Risk consultants define it as policy adherence. Academic centers define it as cognitive partnership. Each is right about a third of the answer. The Future of PMM curriculum is built around all three.

🧠 Thinking with AI

The cognitive dimension. It's the question of whether AI has actually been admitted to your reasoning process — or whether you keep it at arm's length as a faster typist.

Helen Edwards' Cognitive Sovereignty research found that the professionals who reorganized their identity around AI partnership scored highest on every measure of judgment, satisfaction, and output quality — but only when they let AI into the room where the actual thinking happens. The ones who used AI constantly but kept their reasoning walled off scored worst — high tool usage, low cognitive integration.

A PMM who feeds Claude a brief and cleans up the output is operating in what Edwards calls the Creator pattern — using AI heavily, identity unchanged, sovereignty falling. A PMM who runs positioning tests in dialogue with AI, who treats it as a thinking partner with a vote rather than a printer with a delay, is operating as a Framer or Co-author. The 10x PMM thesis lives in this distinction.

🛠️ Hard Skills

The technical dimension — the part most people mean when they say "AI training." Prompting, agent building, tool selection, demo construction, integrating third-party intelligence sources, writing the instructions that turn a Klue battlecard into a Slack-deliverable pre-call brief.

We treat the hard skills as table stakes — not because they're easy, but because the floor for hard-skill fluency is rising fast across the broader PMM labor market, and a year from now anyone competing for a senior product marketing seat will need them.

The curriculum covers prompting, the AI Tool Stack chapter that maps the vendor landscape from generalist LLMs to category-specific agents like Klue and Evertune to internal SAP environments, and the agent-construction sections. Every chapter ends with a Hands-On — a specific build with your own portfolio data that leaves you with a working agent or workflow.

🤝 Soft Skills

The cultural and policy dimensions — the part of AI capability that doesn't show up on a resume but determines whether a PMM organization can actually deploy AI at scale. Three things sit here:

Policy Embedding: SAP has a privacy policy, a security policy, a data classification matrix, a Trust Center, an approved-tool list, and a set of contractual obligations to customers. The curriculum translates these into PMM-specific operating rules. The Maya scenario is what happens when policy embedding isn't part of the curriculum.

Communications about AI: How you talk about your AI use to your manager, cross-functional partners, customers, and analysts is itself a competence. The curriculum includes specific scripts: how to tell a customer that an SAP agent generated the executive summary they're reading, how to explain to a Forrester analyst why your messaging shifted between briefings.

Culture: The set of shared norms about how AI is used inside a team. Whether using Claude for a deck draft is something you brag about or something you hide. Whether the standard of work has actually risen now that the floor has risen. Culture sits in the curriculum as a thread — the Use Case of the Week, office-hours format, and peer-review structure are all designed to expose, name, and reinforce the culture we want.

The key frame: A 10x PMM is not a PMM with the most tools, the cleanest policies, or the highest cognitive sovereignty score. A 10x PMM is a PMM in whom all three dimensions are developing together — where the tool layer extends what the thinking can do, where the cultural layer protects what the thinking has produced, and where the thinking itself has been allowed to become genuinely collaborative.

What This Is

📚 Guided Learning

Each unit builds on the last, with clear objectives and knowledge checks along the way. You will learn not only about AI tools, but how to think and work alongside AI and approach marketing differently.

🛠️ Practical Focus

You will leverage exercises that teach you practical frameworks you can apply to actual products and campaigns. This will change the way you work today.

⏱️ Self-Paced

The total course is about 8 hours total. It comes with online interactive learning units, take-home reading materials, interactive assessments, and is backed by the futureofpmm.com website with many relevant resources.

📅 Weekly Sessions: Every week, we will host a live educational Teams session to teach the curriculum as we go.

Why We Built This

The way SAP's buyers discover, evaluate, and purchase our software has fundamentally changed. AI tools now mediate the research process. Committees make decisions with AI-generated shortlists. The old playbook — launch, enable, wait for leads — no longer works the way it used to.

We will examine the current funnel and our way of working, and suggest what the new agentic marketing funnel looks like – and how SAP can adapt PMM strategies and work to align to it.

This program teaches the skills our PMMs need to drive impact in this new environment.

What You'll Walk Away With

  • A clear understanding of how AI is reshaping B2B buying behavior and what you can do to adapt with AI tools and approaches
  • Practical frameworks for positioning, GTM, and competitive strategy where you can work alongside AI to research, differentiate and deliver powerful messaging and positioning
  • Hands-on experience with exercises you can apply to our own products at SAP
  • Confidence to lead product marketing as an AI-enabled "10X PMM" who doesn't just use tools to do more, but works with AI to work smarter and better

What is Happening More Broadly at SAP

This is our own teams' effort, and other SAP CMO groups are leading their own efforts to test and learn new tools and approaches. Our hope is that we can move quickly, iterate often, learn from your feedback and help SAP become the leader in AI PMM adoption.

🪞 A Moment of Reflection

Before you begin, ask yourself:

Are you more Maya or more Trevor?

Maya had the hard skills — built prompts, ran agentic workflows, moved fast. But she wasn't thinking with AI; she was thinking around it. Trevor understood the policies cold but wasn't using AI to actually extend his capabilities.

Keep this question in mind as you move through the assessments. Your answer will shape which parts of this curriculum matter most for you.
